verdict.summary:
# FMLA entitlement under 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(a) — amount and measuring period

## Answer

| Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| How much FMLA leave is an eligible employee entitled to (excluding covered-servicemember caregiver leave)? | **12 workweeks** — a single aggregate ceiling, not 12 weeks per qualifying reason | 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(a) |
| Over what period? | **Any 12-month period** — specifically, the 12-month period defined by whichever of the four methods in § 825.200(b) the employer has selected and applies uniformly: (1) calendar year; (2) any fixed 12-month leave year; (3) 12-month period measured forward from the first FMLA leave taken under (a); or (4) rolling 12-month period measured backward from each use of FMLA leave under (a) | 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(b)(1)–(4) |

Both figures exclude leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, which carries its own, separate **26-workweek** entitlement under § 825.200(f) and is outside the scope of this answer.

---

## 1. Governing text (quoted verbatim from the fetched sources)

**§ 825.200(a)** — eCFR, https://ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-C/part-825/subpart-B/section-825.200 (fetched 2026-11-17T05:52:41Z, sha256 c09462b269fc):

> "(a) Except in the case of leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, an eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for any one, or more, of the following reasons:
> (1) The birth of the employee's son or daughter, and to care for the newborn child;
> (2) The placement with the employee of a son or daughter for adoption or foster care, and to care for the newly placed child;
> (3) To care for the employee's spouse, son, daughter, or parent with a serious health condition;
> (4) Because of a serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform one or more of the essential functions of his or her job; and,
> (5) Because of any qualifying exigency arising out of the fact that the employee's spouse, son, daughter, or parent is a military member on covered active duty status (or has been notified of an impending call or order to covered active duty)."

**§ 825.200(b)** — same source:

> "(b) An employer is permitted to choose any one of the following methods for determining the 12-month period in which the 12 weeks of leave entitlement described in paragraph (a) of this section occurs:
> (1) The calendar year;
> (2) Any fixed 12-month leave year, such as a fiscal year, a year required by State law, or a year starting on an employee's anniversary date;
> (3) The 12-month period measured forward from the date any employee's first FMLA leave under paragraph (a) begins; or,
> (4) A "rolling" 12-month period measured backward from the date an employee uses any FMLA leave as described in paragraph (a)."

**§ 825.200(h), first sentence** (holiday counting) — govinfo PDF, CFR-2025-title29-vol3-sec825-200.pdf (fetched 2026-11-17T05:52:40Z, sha256 63329212df39):

> "(h) For purposes of determining the amount of leave used by an employee, the fact that a holiday may occur within the week taken as FMLA leave has no effect; the week is counted as a week of FMLA leave."

---

## 2. What § 825.200(a) does and does not say

1. **It is one aggregate ceiling, not a per-reason allowance.** The operative words are "limited to a **total** of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for **any one, or more, of** the following reasons." Leave taken for reason (a)(1) draws down the same 12-week balance that would otherwise be available for reasons (a)(3), (a)(4), or (a)(5). An employee cannot stack 12 weeks for a birth and another 12 weeks for their own serious health condition inside the same 12-month period.
2. **It is a cap, not a floor or a guarantee.** "Limited to" establishes the maximum the employer must make available; the employee is not obliged to use it, and an employer may (subject to other law, a CBA, or its own policy) provide more.
3. **The unit of account is the workweek.** The regulation does not state the entitlement in hours. Arithmetic conversions are derivative only and must be labelled as such: 12 workweeks = 60 workdays for a 5-day workweek (12 × 5) = 480 hours for a 40-hour workweek (12 × 40). For part-time employees, employees with varying schedules, and leave taken in increments of less than a full week, § 825.200 itself cross-refers out: the fetched PDF text states that "Methods for determining an employee's 12-week leave entitlement are also described in § 825.205." **§ 825.205 was not fetched for this analysis** — do not treat any hours figure above as the § 825.205 conversion.
4. **"Eligible employee" is a term of art defined elsewhere.** Section 825.200(a) supplies the *amount* once eligibility exists; it does not restate the eligibility elements (service, hours, worksite/50-employee and 75-mile tests), which live in §§ 825.110–.111. Those sections were not fetched and are not restated here as quoted text.
5. **The introductory carve-out removes only the caregiver entitlement, not the 12-week cap.** The 26-workweek entitlement in § 825.200(f) is excluded from this answer by the terms of the request. But note the interaction preserved in § 825.200(g) and the Part 825 example (govinfo PDF, sha256 2a999ac77e89): "an eligible employee may, during the single 12-month period, take 16 workweeks of FMLA leave to care for a covered servicemember and 10 workweeks of FMLA leave to care for a newborn child. However, the employee may not take more than 12 weeks of FMLA leave to care for the newborn child during the single 12-month period, even if the employee takes fewer than 14 workweeks of FMLA leave to care for a covered servicemember." The 12-week figure in (a) therefore continues to bind even where caregiver leave is also in play.
6. **Holidays do not reduce the count.** Under § 825.200(h), a holiday falling inside a week counted as FMLA leave does not shorten the charge; the week counts as a week.
7. **Two grounded exceptions to the flat "12 workweeks" statement** — flag both, because they change the number for defined populations without changing § 825.200(a):
   - **Airline flight crew employees.** § 825.802(a)(1) (fetched, sha256 0da8b6019556): "An eligible airline flight crew employee is entitled to 72 days of FMLA leave during any 12-month period for one, or more, of the FMLA-qualifying reasons set forth in §§ 825.112(a)(1)-(5). This entitlement is based on a uniform six-day workweek … multiplied by the statutory 12-workweek entitlement." (72 = 6 × 12.)
   - **Spouses employed by the same covered employer.** § 825.201(b) (fetched, sha256 63329212df39) permits limiting the *couple* to a combined total of 12 weeks during any 12-month period for care of a parent, birth/care of a newborn, and placement/care of an adopted or foster child. The entitlement total remains 12; it is shared.

---

## 3. The 12-month period: the four permissible methods

§ 825.200(b) gives the employer — not the employee — the choice, and the choice is what converts "any 12-month period" into a definite window.

| § 825.200(b) | Method | Anchor / trigger | Example of a first measuring period | When the 12-week balance resets |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (1) | Calendar year | January 1 | Jan 1 – Dec 31 | Each January 1 |
| (2) | Any fixed 12-month leave year (fiscal year, State-law year, anniversary date) | The first day of the chosen fixed year | Jul 1 – Jun 30 (fiscal); or anniversary date through the day before the next anniversary | The first day of each successive fixed 12-month year |
| (3) | 12-month period measured **forward** from the date the employee's first FMLA leave under (a) begins | The first day of that employee's first (a) leave — a per-employee anchor | If first leave begins 2025-03-03, the period runs 2025-03-03 through 2026-03-02 | At the end of each 12 months measured from that same anchor |
| (4) | "Rolling" 12-month period measured **backward** from the date the employee uses any FMLA leave under (a) | Each date leave is used — the window slides continuously | On any date D, the window is the 12 months ending on D | Continuously: the balance is 12 weeks minus all (a) leave used in the trailing 12 months ending on the date in question |

**Two points that decide real cases:**

- Methods (3) and (4) are not equivalent. Under (3), a fresh 12 weeks becomes available at the 12-month anniversary of the first leave regardless of how much was used in the preceding months. Under (4), there is no anniversary reset at all; the employee's available balance on any given day depends on usage during the preceding 12 months, so heavy use in one stretch suppresses the balance until that usage ages out of the window.
- The method must be applied consistently and uniformly. The paragraphs immediately following § 825.200(b) — printed as § 825.200(c)–(e) in the current eCFR — govern changing methods (60 days' notice to all employees), uniform application, and the most-beneficial-outcome rule during a transition. The fetched excerpt of those paragraphs is **truncated mid-paragraph**; the only portion captured verbatim is: "During the running of the 60-day period any other employee who needs FMLA leave may use the option providing the most beneficial outcome to that employee. At the conclusion of the 60-day period the employer may implement the selected option." (sha256 63329212df39). The full wording of (c)–(e) — including the default rule if an employer has not selected a method — should be pulled from the complete section text before being quoted in any notice or policy.

---

## 4. Procedure: computing an employee's remaining entitlement

1. **Confirm eligibility** under §§ 825.110–.111 (12 months of service, 1,250 hours in the preceding 12 months, worksite/50-employee/75-mile tests). § 825.200(a)'s 12 weeks applies only to an *eligible* employee.
2. **Confirm the reason** maps to one of § 825.200(a)(1)–(5). If the reason is care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, stop — that is the 26-workweek entitlement under § 825.200(f), expressly excluded here.
3. **Identify the employer's selected 12-month method** under § 825.200(b). Record the selection in writing; it is the dispositive input.
4. **Fix the measurement window** for the date in question using the table in §3 above.
5. **Total the FMLA-designated leave already used** within that window, counting by workweek. Apply § 825.200(h): a holiday inside a counted week does not reduce the charge. For partial weeks, intermittent leave, and reduced schedules, apply the calculation methods in § 825.205 (cross-referenced by § 825.200; **not fetched — verify**).
6. **Subtract** used weeks from 12. The remainder is the balance available in that window. The result can never exceed 12 and never falls below 0.
7. **Apply population-specific overlays** where they fit: 72 days for airline flight crew (§ 825.802(a)(1)); the combined 12-week spousal limit (§ 825.201(b)).
8. **Document the designation** — the employer, not the employee, designates leave as FMLA-qualifying (§ 825.200, as reflected in the fetched Part 825 text describing the employer's designation responsibility under § 825.300).

---

## 5. Worked illustrations

**Rolling backward, method (b)(4).** Employee used 4 workweeks of FMLA leave in March and 3 workweeks in September. On November 1, the trailing 12-month window ending that day contains 4 + 3 = 7 workweeks. Balance = 12 − 7 = **5 workweeks**. If the March absence ages out of the window the following March, the balance rises to 12 − 3 = 9 at that point (assuming no further use).

**Forward, method (b)(3).** Employee's first (a) leave began 2025-03-03. The measuring period is 2025-03-03 through 2026-03-02, and **12 workweeks** are available for use at any point inside it — including, for example, 8 weeks in February 2026 followed by 4 more in early March 2026, provided all fall within the same forward period. A new 12 weeks becomes available on 2026-03-03.

**Fixed calendar year, method (b)(1).** Employee uses all 12 workweeks in November–December 2025. On January 1, 2026, a fresh **12 workweeks** is available, because the calendar year is the window and it has rolled. The same pattern under method (b)(4) would leave the employee with little or no balance in January 2026.

---

## 6. Scope, provenance, and items to verify before operational use

- **Grounded and quoted:** § 825.200(a), (b)(1)–(4), (f), (g), the first sentence of (h), § 825.201(b), § 825.802(a), and the Part 825 example on combining caregiver and newborn leave. All quoted strings above appear verbatim in the fetched sources cited.
- **Not fetched, cited only as cross-references — verify before relying on the wording:** § 825.200(c)–(e) in full (60-day change notice, uniform application, default method); the remainder of § 825.200(h) (partial-week increments); § 825.205 (calculation methods, part-time and varying schedules); §§ 825.110–.111 (eligibility); § 825.127 (military caregiver); § 825.207 (substitution of paid leave — it affects how leave is *paid*, not the 12-workweek *amount*).
- **Arithmetic conversions are derivative, not regulatory text:** 60 workdays (12 × 5), 480 hours (12 × 40), 72 days (6 × 12). The regulation counts in workweeks.
- **This answer states the federal regulatory default.** It does not account for a State or local family-leave statute, a collective bargaining agreement, or an employer policy that provides more than 12 workweeks or defines a different (more generous) measuring period. Where those exist, the employee's actual entitlement may be greater, and the § 825.200(b) method governs only the federal floor.
- **Role note (Legal):** this is an analysis of the text of 29 C.F.R. § 825.200 for design purposes. It is not an opinion on a specific employee's entitlement, which requires that employee's dates, hours, schedule, and the employer's documented method selection.

verdict.summary:
RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1 — Maximum total lengths and exactly what the counts include

=====================================================================
1. DIRECT ANSWER
=====================================================================

| Line type (RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.x) | Maximum total length | Terminator included? |
|---|---|---|
| Text line — §4.5.3.1.6 (line of message content, i.e. inside DATA) | 1000 octets | Yes, CRLF included; the duplicated leading dot is NOT counted |
| Reply line — §4.5.3.1.5 (server → client) | 512 octets | Yes, CRLF included; reply code included |
| (For contrast) Command line — §4.5.3.1.4 (client → server) | 512 octets | Yes, CRLF included; command word included |

Both limits are in OCTETS (8-bit bytes), not characters. RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1 states the figures are expressed "in octets where absolute lengths, rather than character counts, are intended." So a line containing non-ASCII octets (e.g. under 8BITMIME, RFC 6152) is measured by byte count, and UTF-8 multibyte characters consume one octet each of the budget.

=====================================================================
2. VERBATIM RFC TEXT (the normative sentences)
=====================================================================

§4.5.3.1.5.  Reply Line
"The maximum total length of a reply line including the reply code and
the <CRLF> is 512 octets.  More information may be conveyed through
multiple-line replies."

§4.5.3.1.6.  Text Line
"The maximum total length of a text line including the <CRLF> is 1000
octets (not counting the leading dot duplicated for transparency).
This number may be increased by the use of SMTP Service Extensions."

(§4.5.3.1.4.  Command Line — quoted for disambiguation only:
"The maximum total length of a command line including the command word
and the <CRLF> is 512 octets.  SMTP extensions may be used to
increase this limit.")

=====================================================================
3. WHAT THE REPLY-LINE COUNT (512) INCLUDES — OCTET-BY-OCTET
=====================================================================

Included:
  a) The 3-digit reply code — Reply-code = %x32-35 %x30-35 %x30-39 (first digit 2–5, second 0–5, third 0–9).        3 octets
  b) The separator after the code:
       - final line of a reply: <SP> (%d32), which RFC 5321 explicitly
         states "is considered part of the text"                 1 octet
       - non-final line of a multiline reply: "-" (hyphen)      1 octet
  c) The reply text (textstring = 1*(%d09 / %d32-126) — HT, SP,
     printable US-ASCII), i.e. up to 506 octets                 ≤506 octets
  d) The terminating <CRLF>                                    2 octets
                                                               ----------
  Maximum total                                                512 octets

Excluded / not applicable:
  - There is no separate allowance for the CRLF: it is inside the 512.
  - The code is not free: it is inside the 512.
  - A multiline reply does NOT get a 512-octet budget in total. Each
    individual line is separately limited to 512 octets; the reply as a
    whole may be arbitrarily long, which is precisely why §4.5.3.1.5
    says "More information may be conveyed through multiple-line
    replies."

Derived budgets (all consistent with 512):
  - Final line with text:     3 + 1(SP) + 506 + 2 = 512
  - Final line, bare code, no SP and no text (clients MUST accept):
                              3 + 0 + 0 + 2   = 5   (≤512)
  - Final line, no SP but 507 octets of text (clients MUST be prepared
    for the SP to be omitted): 3 + 507 + 2      = 512
  - Non-final line of a multiline reply: 3 + 1("-") + 506 + 2 = 512

=====================================================================
4. WHAT THE TEXT-LINE COUNT (1000) INCLUDES — OCTET-BY-OCTET
=====================================================================

Included:
  a) Every octet of the line's content as it appears after
     transparency removal, including any HT, SP, printable ASCII, and
     any 8-bit octets permitted by an extension (8BITMIME)       ≤998 octets
  b) The terminating <CRLF>                                     2 octets
                                                               ----------
  Maximum total                                                1000 octets

Explicitly excluded:
  - The extra leading "." inserted for dot-stuffing (transparency,
    §4.5.2). The RFC's parenthetical "(not counting the leading dot
    duplicated for transparency)" is the only exclusion. Consequently a
    line whose content begins with "." may be 1001 octets ON THE WIRE
    while its counted length remains 1000.

Not covered by the 1000-octet limit:
  - The terminating ".\r\n" end-of-data sequence is a command/terminator,
    not a text line, and is not charged to the 1000-octet budget.
  - The limit applies to message content lines (header section and body
    alike, both are transmitted as text lines).

Derived budgets (all consistent with 1000):
  - Maximum content before CRLF:            998 octets
  - Same line, first content octet is ".":   wire line = 1 + 998 + 2 = 1001 octets,
                                             counted length = 1000 octets
  - Empty line (just CRLF):                 2 octets (≤1000)

=====================================================================
5. WORKED WIRE-LEVEL EXAMPLES WITH EXACT OCTET COUNTS
=====================================================================

Reply lines
  "250 OK\r\n"                          → 3+1+2+2      =   8 octets   OK
  "250-\r\n" (empty continuation)       → 3+1+0+2      =   6 octets   OK
  "250 " + 506×'x' + "\r\n"             → 3+1+506+2    = 512 octets   AT LIMIT
  "250 " + 507×'x' + "\r\n"             → 3+1+507+2    = 513 octets   OVER — must not be sent
  "250" + 507×'x' + "\r\n" (no SP)      → 3+0+507+2    = 512 octets   AT LIMIT

Text lines
  "Hello\r\n"                           → 5+2          =   7 octets   OK
  998×'x' + "\r\n"                      → 998+2        = 1000 octets  AT LIMIT
  999×'x' + "\r\n"                      → 999+2        = 1001 octets  OVER — must not be sent
  "." + 998×'x' + "\r\n" (content starts with '.') → wire 1001 octets, counted 1000 octets  AT LIMIT

Command lines (for contrast, same 512 arithmetic)
  "QUIT\r\n"                            → 4+2          =   6 octets   OK
  "MAIL FROM:<" + path + ">" + CRLF — path itself ≤256 octets (§4.5.3.1.3), so the whole command is bounded by both limits simultaneously; the binding constraint is whichever is reached first.

=====================================================================
6. RELATED LIMITS IN THE SAME SECTION (context; do not conflate)
=====================================================================

§4.5.3.1.1  Local-part        ≤  64 octets
§4.5.3.1.2  Domain            ≤ 255 octets
§4.5.3.1.3  Path              ≤ 256 octets (including punctuation and element separators)
§4.5.3.1.4  Command line      ≤ 512 octets (including command word and CRLF)
§4.5.3.1.5  Reply line        ≤ 512 octets (including reply code and CRLF)
§4.5.3.1.6  Text line         ≤ 1000 octets (including CRLF, excluding duplicated transparency dot)
§4.5.3.1.7  Message content   ≥ 64K octets (a minimum the receiver must accept, not a maximum)
§4.5.3.1.8  Recipient buffer  ≥ 100 recipients

=====================================================================
7. COMMON MISREADINGS THIS ANSWER FORECLOSES
=====================================================================

1. "Text line = command line." No. §4.5.3.1.6 "Text Line" is a line of message content inside DATA (1000 octets). Command lines are §4.5.3.1.4 (512 octets). Both happen to be asked about often; the numbers differ by design.
2. "512 for the reply includes only the text." No — code, separator and CRLF are all inside the 512.
3. "A multiline reply totals 512." No — each line is independently ≤512; the reply may be many lines long.
4. "The 1000 excludes CRLF." No — CRLF is inside the 1000; only the transparency dot is excluded.
5. "1000 characters." No — 1000 octets. With 8BITMIME/UTF-8 payloads, byte count ≠ character count.
6. "These are hard ceilings for receivers." They are the minimum maximums every implementation MUST accept; SMTP service extensions (e.g. the SIZE/LIMITS family, and §4.5.3.1.6's own note) may raise them, and real implementations commonly accept longer lines. A conforming sender must not exceed them absent a negotiated extension.

=====================================================================
8. RECEIVER IMPLEMENTATION RULE (actionable form)
=====================================================================

- Reply-line reader: read until CRLF; accept up to and including 512 octets. Do not hard-fail at 510 or 511 (that would reject legal bare-code lines with long text and no SP). Treat anything beyond 512 as a protocol violation; truncate or 500-reject rather than buffer unboundedly.
- Text-line reader (DATA state): read until CRLF, remove one leading transparency dot if the line begins with "..", then assert counted length ≤ 1000 octets. Buffer sizing must therefore allow 1001 octets on the wire plus one lookahead octet.
- Command-line reader: same 512-octet ceiling as the reply line, including the verb and CRLF.

Verification arithmetic (self-check, all bounds satisfied):
  3+1+506+2 = 512  ✓ reply line at limit
  4+506+2   = 512  ✓ multiline continuation at limit
  998+2     = 1000 ✓ text line at limit
  1+998+2   = 1001 ✓ wire length with transparency dot, counted length 1000 ✓
No figure quoted above exceeds the limit it is measured against.

quotes.whole:
Editorial Note on Part 395




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 395 appear at 66 FR 49874, Oct. 1, 2001.






§ 395.3 Maximum driving time for property-carrying vehicles.




(a) Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1, no motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, unless the driver complies with the following requirements:




(1) Start of work shift.  A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty;






(2) 14-hour period.  A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty.






(3) Driving time and interruptions of driving periods —




(i) Driving time.  A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.






(ii) Interruption of driving time.  Except for drivers who qualify for either of the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. A consecutive 30-minute interruption of driving status may be satisfied either by off-duty, sleeper berth or on-duty not driving time or by a combination of off-duty, sleeper berth and on-duty not driving time.










(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—




(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any period of 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or






(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.








(c) 




(1) Any period of 7 consecutive days may end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours.





(2) Any period of 8 consecutive days may end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours.





[76 FR 81188, Dec. 27, 2011, as amended at 78 FR 58485, Sept. 24, 2013; 78 FR 64181, Oct. 28, 2013; 84 FR 48081, Sept. 12, 2019; 85 FR 33452, June 1, 2020]

Nomenclature changes to part 395 appear at 66 FR 49874, Oct. 1, 2001.






§ 395.3 Maximum driving time for property-carrying vehicles.




(a) Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1, no motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, unless the driver complies with the following requirements:




(1) Start of work shift.  A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty;






(2) 14-hour period.  A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty.






(3) Driving time and interruptions of driving periods —




(i) Driving time.  A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.






(ii) Interruption of driving time.  Except for drivers who qualify for either of the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. A consecutive 30-minute interruption of driving status may be satisfied either by off-duty, sleeper berth or on-duty not driving time or by a combination of off-duty, sleeper berth and on-duty not driving time.










(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—




(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any period of 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or






(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.








(c) 




(1) Any period of 7 consecutive days may end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours.





(2) Any period of 8 consecutive days may end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours.





[76 FR 81188, Dec. 27, 2011, as amended at 78 FR 58485, Sept. 24, 2013; 78 FR 64181, Oct. 28, 2013; 84 FR 48081, Sept. 12, 2019; 85 FR 33452, June 1, 2020]

verdict.summary:
Scope: This answers the base rule in 49 CFR §395.3(a) for a driver of a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, with no §395.1 exception or waiver invoked. It states the regulatory eligibility-to-drive limits, not a review of a particular driver's record of duty status.

1. Off-duty period required before driving: 10 consecutive hours off duty.
Citation: 49 CFR §395.3(a)(1): 'A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty.' This is the minimum off-duty period that must precede driving at the start of a work shift. It is not the 34-hour period used to reset the 60/70-hour cycle under §395.3(c).

2. End of the driving window: 14 consecutive hours after coming on duty.
Citation: 49 CFR §395.3(a)(2): 'A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty.' The 14-hour clock starts when the driver comes on duty after the qualifying 10 consecutive hours off duty. It is elapsed time, not 14 hours of accumulated on-duty status: an off-duty, sleeper-berth, or on-duty-not-driving break inside the window generally does not extend the 14-hour deadline under the base rule. Driving is no longer permitted at the end of the 14th consecutive hour. Example: if the driver comes on duty at 06:00 after 10 hours off duty, no driving is permitted after 20:00.

3. Total driving permitted within that period: 11 hours.
Citation: 49 CFR §395.3(a)(3)(i): 'A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.' The 11 hours must fit inside the 14-hour window and does not extend the window. In the example above, the driver may drive up to 11 hours between 06:00 and 20:00.

Additional §395.3(a) constraints that do not change the three answers:
- §395.3(a)(3)(ii) requires at least one consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status after more than 8 cumulative hours of driving time, unless a short-haul exception applies. The interruption may be off-duty, sleeper-berth, on-duty-not-driving, or a combination. This can reduce the driving available inside the 11/14-hour limits but does not change the 10, 14, or 11-hour figures.
- §395.3(b) separately prohibits driving after 60 hours on duty in any period of 7 consecutive days if the carrier does not operate every day of the week, or after 70 hours on duty in any period of 8 consecutive days if the carrier operates every day of the week. These weekly limits can stop driving earlier.
- §395.3(c) allows any period of 7 or 8 consecutive days to end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours. That resets the weekly cycle; it does not change the 10-hour before-driving requirement, the 14-hour window, or the 11-hour driving limit.

Caveat on exceptions: §395.1 contains exceptions that can alter the applicable hour figures if their conditions are met. Examples include the §395.1(o) property-carrying 16-hour exception, the §395.1(e) short-haul provisions, the §395.1(b) adverse-driving-conditions provision, and the §395.1(g) sleeper-berth split. Because the request asks under §395.3(a) and does not specify any exception, the answers above are the standard §395.3(a) limits: 10 consecutive hours off duty, 14 consecutive hours after coming on duty, and 11 total hours of driving within that 14-hour period.

1. Rescission period.

verdict.summary:
MEMORANDUM — Rescission deadline under 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i)

1. ANSWER

(1) General rule. The consumer may exercise the right to rescind "until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last." The trigger is therefore the LAST of three events, not consummation alone, and the deadline is midnight at the end of the third business day counted from that last event.

(2) Never-delivered branch. "If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first." The outer limit is three years after consummation, cut short by a transfer of all of the consumer's interest or by a sale of the property.

2. GOVERNING TEXT (12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i), as currently published on eCFR and as confirmed unchanged in the 2021 printed CFR)

"(3)(i) The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act."

Two textual points that control the analysis and are frequently gotten wrong:

(a) The regulation contains no "one year after sale" rule. The expiration events are transfer of all of the consumer's interest, or sale of the property — full stop, with no grace period. Any workflow, checklist or system rule that encodes a one-year post-sale rescission tail under § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) is wrong and should be removed.

(b) The three-year figure is measured in years from consummation, not in business days, and it is not the same clock as the three-business-day window. The three-business-day window is the general rule; the three-year period is the consequence of non-delivery.

3. ASK 1 — HOW TO COMPUTE THE THREE-BUSINESS-DAY DEADLINE

3.1 Identify the three candidate events

- Consummation of the transaction (for open-end plans under § 1026.15, the occurrence giving rise to the right).
- Delivery of the notice required by § 1026.23(b): two copies to each consumer entitled to rescind (one copy each if delivered electronically in compliance with E-Sign), on a separate document identifying the transaction, disclosing the security interest, the right to rescind, how to exercise it with the form and the creditor's address, the effects of rescission, and the date the rescission period expires.
- Delivery of all material disclosures. Per § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii), "material disclosures" means the required disclosures of the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g).

3.2 Take the latest of the three dates. The period does not begin to run until the last of them has occurred. Official interpretation ¶ 23(b)(1)-4 (Time of providing notice) states the notice need not be given before consummation, but "the rescission period will not begin to run until the notice is given": if the creditor provides the notice on May 15 but disclosures were given and the transaction consummated on May 10, the three-business-day period runs from May 15.

3.3 Count three business days forward from that date, excluding the trigger day itself. Use the rescission-specific business-day definition of § 1026.2(a)(6) (all calendar days except Sundays and the legal public holidays specified in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a)), not the "offices open" definition. That Saturdays count is confirmed arithmetically by the CFPB commentary examples: where consummation is Friday, June 1, and the disclosures and rescission notice were given Thursday, May 31, the period "will expire at midnight of the third business day after June 1 — that is, Tuesday, June 5" (Saturday June 2 = day 1, Monday June 4 = day 2, Tuesday June 5 = day 3); and where disclosures and consummation are Friday, June 1, with the rescission notice given Monday, June 4, the period expires "at midnight of the third business day after June 4 — that is, Thursday, June 7."

3.4 The deadline is midnight at the end of that third business day. Note that midnight is not further defined in the text quoted; where a transaction spans time zones, record the consumer's location and the creditor's receipt cut-off in the file rather than assuming.

3.5 Exercise is effective on dispatch, not receipt. Under § 1026.23(a)(2) the consumer notifies the creditor "by mail, telegram or other means of written communication," and notice "is considered given when mailed, when filed for telegraphic transmission or, if sent by other means, when delivered to the creditor's designated place of business." A notice mailed before midnight on the final day is timely even though it arrives later.

3.6 Multiple consumers. Section 1026.23(b)(1) requires delivery of the notice to each consumer entitled to rescind, and § 1026.23(a)(4) provides that "the exercise of the right by one consumer shall be effective as to all consumers." Practical consequence for a compliance system: compute the anchor date per consumer entitled to rescind (each consumer's own notice/material-disclosure delivery dates), and treat the earliest resulting deadline among them as the operative date on which the right can still be exercised by anyone, because one timely rescission voids the transaction for all.

4. ASK 2 — THE NEVER-DELIVERED BRANCH

4.1 If the § 1026.23(b) notice or the material disclosures are never delivered, the right does not lapse after three business days; it "shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first." Operationally: deadline = earliest of (i) the third anniversary of consummation, (ii) the date all of the consumer's interest in the property is transferred, (iii) the date the property is sold.

4.2 "Never delivered" means delivered neither at consummation nor at any later point. If the notice or material disclosures are delivered late — after consummation but before the three-year point — the three-business-day window restarts and runs from that later delivery (interpretation ¶ 23(b)(1)-4, quoted above). The three-year provision is written for the case where delivery does not happen at all; where delivery happens late, the operative measurement is three business days from the late delivery, and the three-year period functions as the outside limit (15 U.S.C. 1635(f); Jesinoski v. Countrywide Home Loans, Inc., 574 U.S. 259 (2015) — written notice within the period, not suit, effects rescission; the case authority is cited as background and is not part of the fetched regulation text).

4.3 One statutory extension is preserved inside the same sentence: "In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act." Flag any file involving a government-ordered or administrative rescission for that extension rather than applying the three-year figure mechanically.

5. THRESHOLD QUESTIONS THAT MUST BE ANSWERED BEFORE EITHER DATE IS COMPUTED

- Does the right exist at all? Section 1026.23(f) exempts residential mortgage transactions, refinancings/consolidations by the same creditor of credit already secured by the principal dwelling (except as to the excess amount financed), transactions in which a state agency is the creditor, certain subsequent advances in a series, and renewals of optional insurance premiums. No rescission deadline applies where there is no right.
- Was the right waived? Section 1026.23(e) permits a waiver in a personal financial emergency; a valid waiver ends the analysis.
- Is the three-business-day deadline measured against accurate disclosures? Sections 1026.23(g) (tolerances) and (h) (inaccurate or incomplete disclosures) bear on whether what was delivered counts as delivery of the material disclosures. The text of (g)–(h) was not part of the passages retrieved for this memorandum, so those provisions are identified as cross-references to be read in full before a file is closed as "disclosures delivered."
- Is the transaction open-end? Section 1026.15(a)(3) contains the parallel three-business-day / three-year structure for open-end plans, with the trigger being the occurrence that gives rise to the right. The analysis above maps onto it, but the citation for an open-end file should be § 1026.15, not § 1026.23.

6. DECISION PROCEDURE (implementable as written)

    rescissionDeadline(consummationDate, noticeDelivered, materialDisclosuresDelivered, transferAllInterestDate, saleDate, administrativeProceeding):
        if rightDoesNotApply under 23(f) or validWaiver under 23(e): return NO_RIGHT
        if noticeDelivered is NEVER or materialDisclosuresDelivered is NEVER:
            candidates = [ consummationDate + 3 years, transferAllInterestDate, saleDate ]   # ignore nulls
            deadline = earliest(candidates)
        else:
            anchor = max(consummationDate, latestNoticeDelivery, latestMaterialDisclosureDelivery)
            deadline = midnight at end of nthBusinessDay(after = anchor, n = 3)
                       # businessDay = Mon-Sat minus Sundays and 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) holidays
        if administrativeProceeding: apply 15 U.S.C. 1635(f) extension per sentence 3 of 23(a)(3)(i)
        return deadline

7. WORKED ILLUSTRATIONS (from the official interpretation)

- Consummation Friday, June 1; notice and material disclosures delivered Thursday, May 31 → anchor = June 1 → third business day = Tuesday, June 5 → deadline: midnight, Tuesday, June 5.
- Consummation and material disclosures Friday, June 1; notice delivered Monday, June 4 → anchor = June 4 → third business day = Thursday, June 7 → deadline: midnight, Thursday, June 7.
- Notice or material disclosures never delivered; consummation March 10, 2022; no transfer or sale → right expires March 10, 2025. If all of the consumer's interest is transferred, or the property is sold, on any earlier date, the right expires on that date instead.

8. CORRECTIONS TO THE PROJECT'S ASSUMPTION TABLE

- The assumption that a further expiration applies "not later than one year after sale or transfer of the interest" is not supported by § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) as published on eCFR or in the 2021 CFR volume. The regulation's expiration events on transfer/sale are immediate, not one year later. That assumption is dropped.
- The assumption that the question turns on the general rule rather than a dated fact pattern is adopted: the answers above are the rule as written, and any live file must supply the actual consummation, delivery, transfer and sale dates to produce a calendar date.
- "Business day" does matter to ask 1 (it is the unit of the three-day window and determines whether a Saturday counts) and does not matter to ask 2 (measured in years). Both are handled above.

quotes.whole:
§ 20.1201 Occupational dose limits for adults.




(a) The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits.




(1) An annual limit, which is the more limiting of—




(i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or






(ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).








(2) The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are:




(i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and






(ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity.










(b) Doses received in excess of the annual limits, including doses received during accidents, emergencies, and planned special exposures, must be subtracted from the limits for planned special exposures that the individual may receive during the current year (see § 20.1206(e)(1)) and during the individual's lifetime (see § 20.1206(e)(2)).






(c) When the external exposure is determined by measurement with an external personal monitoring device, the deep-dose equivalent must be used in place of the effective dose equivalent, unless the effective dose equivalent is determined by a dosimetry method approved by the NRC. The assigned deep-dose equivalent must be for the part of the body receiving the highest exposure. The assigned shallow-dose equivalent must be the dose averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure. The deep-dose equivalent, lens-dose equivalent, and shallow-dose equivalent may be assessed from surveys or other radiation measurements for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with the occupational dose limits, if the individual monitoring device was not in the region of highest potential exposure, or the results of individual monitoring are unavailable.






(d) Derived air concentration (DAC) and annual limit on intake (ALI) values are presented in table 1 of appendix B to part 20 and may be used to determine the individual's dose (see § 20.2106) and to demonstrate compliance with the occupational dose limits.






(e) In addition to the annual dose limits, the licensee shall limit the soluble uranium intake by an individual to 10 milligrams in a week in consideration of chemical toxicity (see footnote 3 of appendix B to part 20).





(f) The licensee shall reduce the dose that an individual may be allowed to receive in the current year by the amount of occupational dose received while employed by any other person (see § 20.2104(e)).



[56 FR 23396, May 21, 1991, as amended at 60 FR 20185, Apr. 25, 1995; 63 FR 39482, July 23, 1998; 67 FR 16304, Apr. 5, 2002; 72 FR 68059, Dec. 4, 2007]

        § 20.1201
        Occupational dose limits for adults.
        
(a) The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits.

        
(1) An annual limit, which is the more limiting of—

        
(i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or

        
(ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).

        
(2) The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are:

        
(i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and

        
(ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity.

        
(b) Doses received in excess of the annual limits, including doses received during accidents, emergencies, and planned special exposures, must be subtracted from the limits for planned special exposures that the individual may receive during the current year (see § 20.1206(e)(1)) and during the individual's lifetime (see § 20.1206(e)(2)).

        

            (c) When the external exposure is determined by measurement with an external personal monitoring device, the deep-dose equivalent must be used in place of the effective dose equivalent, unless the effective dose equivalent is determined by a dosimetry method approved by the NRC. The assigned deep-dose equivalent must be for the part of the body receiving the highest exposure. The assigned shallow-dose equivalent must be the dose averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure. The deep-dose equivalent, lens-dose equivalent, and shallow-dose equivalent may be assessed from surveys or other radiation measurements for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with the occupational dose limits, if the individual monitoring device was not in the region of highest potential exposure, or the results of individual monitoring are unavailable.
            
        

        
(d) Derived air concentration (DAC) and annual limit on intake (ALI) values are presented in table 1 of appendix B to part 20 and may be used to determine the individual's dose (see § 20.2106) and to demonstrate compliance with the occupational dose limits.

        
(e) In addition to the annual dose limits, the licensee shall limit the soluble uranium intake by an individual to 10 milligrams in a week in consideration of chemical toxicity (see footnote 3 of appendix B to part 20).

        
(f) The licensee shall reduce the dose that an individual may be allowed to receive in the current year by the amount of occupational dose received while employed by any other person (see § 20.2104(e)).

verdict.summary:
ANNUAL OCCUPATIONAL DOSE LIMITS FOR ADULT RADIATION WORKERS — 10 CFR § 20.1201(a)

Controlling source: 10 CFR § 20.1201, 'Occupational dose limits for adults,' paragraph (a). Verified against four authoritative renderings that agree verbatim: eCFR current (title 10, chapter I, part 20, subpart C, § 20.1201, fetched 2026-11-17), eCFR subpart C page, GPO CFR 2025 title 10 vol. 1 PDF (sec. 20-1201), and GPO CFR 2024 title 10 vol. 1 XML. Source note on the section: 56 FR 23396, May 21, 1991, as amended at 60 FR 20185 (Apr. 25, 1995); 63 FR 39482 (July 23, 1998); 67 FR 16304 (Apr. 5, 2002); 72 FR 68059 (Dec. 4, 2007). No amendment to paragraph (a) after Dec. 4, 2007 appears in any of the four renderings; the 91 FR 15772 (Mar. 30, 2026) amendment visible in Subpart F touches § 20.1501(d), not § 20.1201(a).

1. THE THREE REQUESTED LIMITS

| Quantity | Regulatory term (citation) | Limit (rems) | Limit (sieverts) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total effective dose equivalent | TEDE — § 20.1201(a)(1)(i) | 5 rem | 0.05 Sv |
| Lens of the eye | Lens dose equivalent — § 20.1201(a)(2)(i) | 15 rem | 0.15 Sv |
| Skin of the whole body | Shallow-dose equivalent — § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii) | 50 rem | 0.5 Sv |

Regulation text, quoted exactly:

§ 20.1201(a): 'The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits.'

§ 20.1201(a)(1): 'An annual limit, which is the more limiting of — (i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or (ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).'

§ 20.1201(a)(2): 'The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are: (i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and (ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity.'

2. UNIT CONVENTION
All conversions use the exact conventional relation 1 rem = 0.01 Sv (1 Sv = 100 rem), which is the convention the regulation itself uses parenthetically: 5 rems (0.05 Sv); 15 rems (0.15 Sv); 50 rem (0.5 Sv). Arithmetic check: 5 x 0.01 = 0.05; 15 x 0.01 = 0.15; 50 x 0.01 = 0.50. No rounding is involved; each Sv figure is exact under that convention.

3. HOW EACH LIMIT IS INTERPRETED AND APPLIED (necessary to use the numbers correctly)
- TEDE, 5 rem/yr: the total effective dose equivalent, i.e., the sum of the deep-dose equivalent from external exposure and the committed effective dose equivalent from intakes of radioactive material (§ 20.1003 definitions; summation rules in § 20.1202). It is the primary whole-body limit.
- Lens of the eye, 15 rem/yr: a lens dose equivalent, assessed at the lens depth (typically Hp(0.3)). It is a separate limit and is expressly excluded from the TEDE/organ summation (§ 20.1202 note: 'The dose equivalents for the lens of the eye, the skin, and the extremities are not included in the summation, but are subject to separate limits').
- Skin of the whole body, 50 rem/yr: a shallow-dose equivalent (typically Hp(0.07)), and per § 20.1201(c) it 'must be the dose averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure' — i.e., a 50 rem limit on a 1 cm²-averaged-at-10-cm² basis, not a uniform whole-body surface average.
- The three limits are concurrent, not additive: a worker may be at the TEDE limit while the lens and skin are separately governed by their own numbers.

4. TWO 50-rem FIGURES — DO NOT CONFLATE
The number 50 rem appears twice in § 20.1201(a) with different meanings:
- § 20.1201(a)(1)(ii): 50 rems (0.5 Sv) = deep-dose equivalent PLUS committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue OTHER THAN THE LENS, as the alternative branch of the 'more limiting of' test in (a)(1). This is NOT the TEDE limit and is outside the three items requested.
- § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii): 50 rem (0.5 Sv) = shallow-dose equivalent to the SKIN of the whole body or of any extremity. This is the requested skin limit.
The TEDE limit is 5 rem, never 50 rem.

5. SCOPE BOUNDARIES (stated so the three numbers are not misapplied)
In scope and answered: the three limits named in the request.
Deliberately not answered, because the request names only TEDE, lens, and whole-body skin: the organ/tissue branch of (a)(1)(ii); the skin-of-extremities limit (same 50 rem value as skin of whole body, but a distinct quantity); planned special exposure allowances (§ 20.1206: 5 x annual limit in a lifetime, and the (e)(1)/(e)(2) subtraction rules); minors at 10% of adult limits (§ 20.1207); the declared-pregnant-worker limit of 0.5 rem to the embryo/fetus (§ 20.1208); and the public dose limit (§ 20.1301).
Note for practice, not part of the numeric answer: these are limits, not goals — § 20.1101 requires ALARA below them; § 20.1502 triggers individual monitoring at 10% of the § 20.1201(a) limits; § 20.1201(f) requires reducing the current-year allowance by occupational dose received while employed by any other person; § 20.1201(b) requires subtracting doses in excess of the annual limits from planned-special-exposure allowances.

No state-agreement or historical variant is represented. If a specific as-of date or a state-analog rule (e.g., an Agreement State adoption with a different lens limit) governs the reader's program, that must be checked against that jurisdiction's rule; the federal figures are as stated here.

verdict.summary:
# Fall Protection Trigger and Required Systems — 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1)

## 1. Direct answer

| Item | Answer |
|---|---|
| Trigger height (Ask 1) | **6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level** |
| Required protection (Ask 2) | **Guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems** (employer may choose any one or more of the three) |

## 2. Controlling regulatory text (verbatim)

**29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1) — Unprotected sides and edges:**

> "Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems."

Source verified against: eCFR 29 CFR 1926.501 (current); GovInfo CFR 2025 Title 29 Vol. 8 § 1926.501; CFR 2024 and CFR 2023 XML editions of the same section. The operative sentence is textually identical in all editions checked (2023, 2024, 2025), i.e., the 6-ft trigger is stable current law.

## 3. How the trigger is applied (procedure)

1. **Identify the walking/working surface.** The parenthetical in the standard is explicit: horizontal *and vertical* surfaces both count. Formwork faces, structural members used as walkways, and similar vertical surfaces are within (b)(1) unless a more specific paragraph of (b) applies.
2. **Identify the unprotected side or edge.** An edge is unprotected if there is no guardrail system, safety net system, personal fall arrest system, cover, or other § 1926.502-compliant barrier between the employee and the drop. A perimeter with a compliant guardrail is not an "unprotected" edge.
3. **Measure to the lower level.** Measure vertically from the walking/working surface on which the employee stands to the surface the employee would strike — the *lowest* level to which the employee is exposed at that edge, not merely the level immediately below. Where an employee is exposed to more than one lower level from the same edge, the lowest governs. The metric equivalent in the standard is 1.8 m.
4. **Apply the threshold.** At **6 ft (1.8 m) or more**, protection is mandatory. Below 6 ft, (b)(1) does not require it (other paragraphs of § 1926.501 may still apply — see § 5).
5. **Select and install a system** from the three named in (b)(1), built to the criteria in § 1926.502 (see § 4).
6. **Document** the measurement, the selected system, and the installation/inspection records.

## 4. The three permitted systems and their governing criteria

The statute permits **any** of the three; it does not rank them or require a specific one. Each must satisfy its criteria in § 1926.502:

| System | Criteria paragraph | Representative design requirements |
|---|---|---|
| Guardrail system | § 1926.502(b) | Top edge height of top rail 42 in ± 3 in above the walking/working surface; midrail, screening, or equivalent protection between top rail and surface; capable of withstanding a 200-lb force applied in any outward or downward direction at any point along the top edge |
| Safety net system | § 1926.502(c) | Installed as close as practicable below the working surface and in no case more than 30 ft (9.1 m) below it; drop-tested or certified; unobstructed fall path into the net; inspected weekly and after any impact |
| Personal fall arrest system | § 1926.502(d) | Full-body harness; anchorage capable of supporting 5,000 lb per employee attached, or designed/installed under supervision of a qualified person as part of a complete system with a safety factor of at least 2; maximum deceleration distance 3.5 ft (1.1 m); no free fall in excess of 6 ft; prompt rescue capability |

*Note on citation precision:* the § 1926.502 paragraph letters above (b)/(c)/(d) are certain; the subparagraph numbers for the 42-in rail, 5,000-lb anchorage, 3.5-ft deceleration, and 30-ft net placement should be re-verified against the current § 1926.502 text before being quoted in an enforcement or citation document.

## 5. What (b)(1) does NOT provide — and what changes the answer

- **No infeasibility exception.** § 1926.501(b)(1) has no exception for infeasible or greater-hazard conditions, and it does not authorize substitution of a § 1926.502(k) fall protection plan. That alternative exists in the standard only where a paragraph grants it — e.g., **leading edges under § 1926.501(b)(2)(i)** — and there the employer bears the burden of establishing infeasibility, with a presumption that at least one listed system is feasible and will not create a greater hazard. **Do not apply the (k) plan option to a plain (b)(1) unprotected side or edge.**
- **More specific paragraphs of (b) displace (b)(1).** Where the exposure fits a specific paragraph, that paragraph's requirements govern; (b)(15) is the residual catch-all and applies only to walking/working surfaces not addressed by (b)(1) through (b)(14). Relevant quoted examples, all keyed to the same 6-ft (1.8 m) trigger but with differing permitted systems:
  - **(b)(2)(i) Leading edges** — 6 ft or more: guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest; infeasibility exception with a § 1926.502(k) plan.
  - **(b)(8) Dangerous equipment** — under 6 ft: guardrail systems or equipment guards; 6 ft or more: guardrail, personal fall arrest, or safety net.
  - **(b)(9) Overhand bricklaying** — 6 ft or more: guardrail, safety net, personal fall arrest, **or a controlled access zone**.
  - **(b)(14) Wall openings** — outside bottom edge 6 ft or more above lower levels and inside bottom edge less than 39 in (1.0 m) above the walking/working surface: guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest.
  - **(b)(15) Walking/working surfaces not otherwise addressed** — 6 ft or more: guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest.
- **Scope exclusions.** § 1926.501(b)(15) expressly excepts workplaces covered by § 1926.500(a)(2). Confirm the activity is within Subpart M's scope before applying (b)(1).
- **Other thresholds in other subparts are separate and higher, and are NOT (b)(1).** Scaffold work under Subpart L and steel erection under Subpart R carry their own trigger heights (10 ft and 15 ft respectively). Those are different rules for different scopes; they neither raise nor lower the 6-ft (1.8 m) trigger of § 1926.501(b)(1). Do not blend them.

## 6. Verification checklist (for a competent engineer applying this)

- [ ] Edge identified and confirmed unprotected (no compliant guardrail, net, PFAS, or cover).
- [ ] Vertical distance measured from the working surface to the **lowest** exposed lower level.
- [ ] Distance recorded as ≥ 6 ft (1.8 m) or < 6 ft (1.8 m).
- [ ] If ≥ 6 ft: system chosen from the three in (b)(1) and verified against § 1926.502(b)/(c)/(d).
- [ ] Confirmed that no more specific paragraph of § 1926.501(b) governs (leading edge, dangerous equipment, overhand bricklaying, wall opening, etc.).
- [ ] Confirmed no § 1926.500(a)(2) scope exclusion applies.
- [ ] If a fall protection plan is being used, confirmed the governing paragraph actually authorizes it (it is not authorized by (b)(1) alone).

## 7. Bottom line

Under 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), an employee on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is **6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level** must be protected from falling by **a guardrail system, a safety net system, or a personal fall arrest system** — the employer's choice among the three, each built to § 1926.502 criteria.

4.—(1) Subject to regulation 5, a worker’s working time, including overtime, in any reference period which is applicable in his case shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days.
(2) An employer shall take all reasonable steps, in keeping with the need to protect the health and safety of workers, to ensure that the limit specified in paragraph (1) is complied with in the case of each worker employed by him in relation to whom it applies.

(a)where a relevant agreement provides for the application of this regulation in relation to successive periods of 17 weeks, each such period, or
(b)in any other case, any period of 17 weeks in the course of his employment.
(4) Where a worker has worked for his employer for less than 17 weeks, the reference period applicable in his case is the period that has elapsed since he started work for his employer.

verdict.summary:
SCOPE AND STATUS
This is a legal summary, not legal advice. It addresses the Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833) as they apply in England and Wales and Scotland (the regulations are marked E+W+S). Northern Ireland has parallel working time regulations and is outside this note. The note is based on the text of reg 4 and reg 5 as made and subsequently amended; before relying on it, check the latest revised version on legislation.gov.uk for any amendments after the version consulted.

1. THE LIMIT: 48 HOURS AVERAGE PER SEVEN DAYS, OVERTIME INCLUDED
Regulation 4(1) provides that, unless the employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work (the original wording was 'Subject to regulation 5'), a worker's working time, including overtime, in any reference period applicable in the worker's case shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days.

Key points:
- The figure is 48 hours. It is an average over the reference period, not a hard cap of 48 hours in every single week. A worker may work more than 48 hours in a particular week provided the average over the applicable reference period does not exceed 48 hours per seven days.
- The ordinary reference period is 17 weeks (reg 4(3)). If the worker has worked for the employer for less than 17 weeks, the reference period is the period since the worker started (reg 4(4)).
- For a worker excluded from the scope of certain provisions by regulation 21, the 17-week references are replaced by 26 weeks (reg 4(5)).
- A relevant agreement under regulation 23(b) may modify the reference period; reg 4(3) is expressly subject to such an agreement.
- The average is calculated under reg 4(6) using the formula (A + B) / C, where A is the aggregate hours of working time in the reference period, B is the aggregate hours in the subsequent period ending when the number of days worked equals the number of excluded days, and C is the number of weeks in the reference period. Excluded days under reg 4(7) include annual leave under reg 13, sick leave, maternity leave (and, as amended, paternity, adoption or parental leave), and periods in respect of which the reg 4(1) limit did not apply because of a reg 5 opt-out agreement.
- The employer must take all reasonable steps, in keeping with the need to protect health and safety, to ensure that the reg 4(1) limit is complied with for each worker to whom it applies (reg 4(2)).

2. HOW A WORKER IS TAKEN OUTSIDE THE LIMIT: THE REGULATION 5 WRITTEN AGREEMENT
Regulation 5(1) provides that the reg 4(1) limit shall not apply in relation to a worker who has agreed with the employer in writing that it should not apply in the worker's case, provided the employer complies with reg 5(4). This is commonly called the individual opt-out.

The operative steps are:
(a) The employer must first obtain the worker's agreement in writing. The current reg 4(1) wording requires the employer to have 'first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work'. An implied, informal or purely collective agreement is not sufficient for reg 5; the individual worker must have agreed in writing.
(b) The agreement may relate to a specified period or apply indefinitely (reg 5(2)(a)).
(c) The worker may terminate the agreement by giving not less than seven days' notice in writing to the employer, subject to any provision in the agreement for a different period of notice (reg 5(2)(b)). Where the agreement provides for termination after a period of notice, that notice period must not exceed three months (reg 5(3)).
(d) The employer must comply with the record-keeping requirements in reg 5(4). The employer must maintain up-to-date records which: identify each worker who has agreed that the reg 4(1) limit should not apply; set out the terms on which the worker so agreed; and specify the number of hours worked by that worker for the employer during each reference period since the agreement came into effect, excluding any period which ended more than two years before the most recent entry in the records. The employer must permit any inspector appointed by the Health and Safety Executive or any other authority responsible under reg 28 for enforcement to inspect those records on request, and must provide such an inspector with such information as may be requested regarding any case in which a worker has agreed that the limit should not apply.
(e) If the employer does not comply with reg 5(4), the reg 5(1) exclusion is not made out. The opt-out must be genuine and voluntary; an employer should not treat a worker's refusal to agree as a breach of contract or as a ground for detriment.

Effect: while a valid reg 5 agreement is in force, the reg 4(1) average limit does not apply to that worker. The opt-out does not remove the separate night-work limits, rest entitlements, annual leave rights, or the employer's general health and safety duties. Special limits apply to young workers (under 18), and those are outside this note.

3. OTHER ROUTES OUTSIDE REG 4(1) (NOT INDIVIDUAL OPT-OUTS)
- Regulation 21 contains category-based exclusions from certain provisions, for example workers whose working time is not measured or predetermined or can be determined by the worker themselves, and certain other categories specified in reg 21. Those workers are outside the relevant provisions by status, not by a reg 5 agreement.
- A relevant agreement under reg 23(b) may modify the reference period, but it does not remove the 48-hour average limit.
- Sector-specific derogations in Part III of the Regulations may apply to particular categories of worker; those are separate from the reg 5 individual opt-out.

In short: the limit is an average of 48 hours per seven days, overtime included, over the applicable reference period (ordinarily 17 weeks); the individual route by which a worker is taken outside reg 4(1) is a prior written agreement with the employer under reg 5, supported by the reg 5(4) records, terminable by the worker on at least seven days' written notice (subject to any different notice period, which cannot exceed three months).

quotes.whole:
§ 211.180 General requirements.




(a) Any production, control, or distribution record that is required to be maintained in compliance with this part and is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the batch.






(b) Records shall be maintained for all components, drug product containers, closures, and labeling for at least 1 year after the expiration date or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the last lot of drug product incorporating the component or using the container, closure, or labeling.






(c) All records required under this part, or copies of such records, shall be readily available for authorized inspection during the retention period at the establishment where the activities described in such records occurred. These records or copies thereof shall be subject to photocopying or other means of reproduction as part of such inspection. Records that can be immediately retrieved from another location by computer or other electronic means shall be considered as meeting the requirements of this paragraph.






(d) Records required under this part may be retained either as original records or as true copies such as photocopies, microfilm, microfiche, or other accurate reproductions of the original records. Where reduction techniques, such as microfilming, are used, suitable reader and photocopying equipment shall be readily available.






(e) Written records required by this part shall be maintained so that data therein can be used for evaluating, at least annually, the quality standards of each drug product to determine the need for changes in drug product specifications or manufacturing or control procedures. Written procedures shall be established and followed for such evaluations and shall include provisions for:




(1) A review of a representative number of batches, whether approved or rejected, and, where applicable, records associated with the batch.






(2) A review of complaints, recalls, returned or salvaged drug products, and investigations conducted under § 211.192 for each drug product.







(f) Procedures shall be established to assure that the responsible officials of the firm, if they are not personally involved in or immediately aware of such actions, are notified in writing of any investigations conducted under §§ 211.198, 211.204, or 211.208 of these regulations, any recalls, reports of inspectional observations issued by the Food and Drug Administration, or any regulatory actions relating to good manufacturing practices brought by the Food and Drug Administration.



[43 FR 45077, Sept. 29, 1978, as amended at 60 FR 4091, Jan. 20, 1995]
